Sobel emphasizes local gradients. Canny adds smoothing and connectivity.

3 × 3 horizontal and vertical filters

Magnitude = |Gx| + |Gy|

16-bit output, zero outer border

5 × 5 smoothing
Gradient and direction
Nonmaximum suppression
Thresholds: 40 / 100
8-connected hysteresis
Canny’s hysteresis queue remains serial in the OpenMP implementation.

Explain, 45 seconds: Sobel work depends only on nearby input pixels, making row and pixel parallelism straightforward. Canny has several stages and requires global connectivity in hysteresis. The implementation parallelizes smoothing, gradients and suppression, while retaining a serial queue for connectivity. This is a documented Canny variant, not a claim of identical behavior to every library.

CPU threads process
separate image rows.

GPU threads compute
output pixels in parallel.

CPU and GPU own separate rows.
A halo row supplies boundary input.
Hybrid uses eight CPU threads and a configurable CPU row fraction.

Explain, 45 seconds: OpenMP uses static row schedules. CUDA uses GPU thread blocks. The hybrid CPU and GPU regions write disjoint output rows, while the GPU receives one preceding halo row for its stencil. Input is immutable. Enqueuing GPU work before CPU work alone does not prove overlap. Use the recorded results rather than claiming automatic simultaneous utilization.

title: A fast kernel is only part of GPU latency

text: A fast kernel is only part of GPU latency
Staging, transfers, computation, synchronization and merge
File I/O, context startup and reusable workspace allocation

Explain, 45 seconds: CUDA event time measures the kernel interval. Host wall time captures the broader processing pipeline. Transfer and staging costs help explain why a very fast kernel does not yield the best overall latency. These are separate medians, so do not treat their subtraction as an exact additive timing breakdown. Canny timing includes its intermediate allocations, which differs from Sobel.

Questions about implementation, correctness or performance
Why can the CPU beat the GPU?
Why can shared memory be slower?
When could a CPU–GPU split help?

Viva answers: CPU vs GPU: Transfers, staging and coordination contribute to latency, and a multicore CPU can be strong on this workload. Shared memory: Halo loads and barriers have costs; observed timings must decide whether tiling helps. Hybrid: A suitable partition may balance work, but overhead and imbalance can erase the gain. This run does not establish a hybrid advantage over OpenMP-8. Why a halo? A 3 by 3 stencil needs one neighboring input row at the partition boundary. Why serial hysteresis? To preserve global edge connectivity. Is this novel edge detection? No, it is a characterization of execution strategies.
